prompt: Four chocolate bars cost 6 EUR more than one chocolate bar. What is the cost of one chocolate bar?

solutions.title: Take away one bar
solutions.body:
Four bars minus one bar is three bars, and that difference is 6 EUR. So three bars cost 6 EUR and one bar costs $6 \div 3 = 2$ EUR.

**Answer: (B) 2 EUR**

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
Let one bar cost $x$. Then $4x = x + 6$, so $3x = 6$ and $x = 2$.

**Answer: (B) 2 EUR**

prompt: From the top of a lighthouse, a kangaroo can see as far as 5 km. How far can 10 kangaroos see from the top of the same lighthouse?

solutions.title: Read carefully
solutions.body:
How far you can see depends on the height of the lighthouse, not on how many kangaroos are looking. Each of the 10 kangaroos still sees 5 km.

**Answer: (A) 5 km**

prompt: A watch is placed face up on a table so that its minute hand points north-east. How many minutes pass before the minute hand points north-west for the first time?

Mary has a pair of scissors and five cardboard letters. She cuts each letter exactly once (along a straight line) so that it falls apart in as many pieces as possible. Which letter falls apart into the most pieces?
A dragon has five heads. Every time a head is chopped off, five new heads grow. If six heads are chopped off one by one, how many heads will the dragon finally have?
In which of the following expressions can we replace each occurrence of the number 8 by the same positive number (other than 8), and obtain the same result?
Each of the nine paths in a park is 100 m long. Ann wants to go from A to B without going along any path more than once. What is the length of the longest route she can choose?

Alice lies on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays and tells the truth on every other day. Bob lies on Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays, and tells the truth on every other day. One day, Alice said: "Today is Monday" and Bob confirmed: "Yes, it is true". Which day of the week was it?

solutions.title: Is Alice telling the truth?
solutions.body:
If Alice told the truth, today would be Monday – but on Mondays Alice lies. Contradiction. So Alice is lying: today is **not** Monday, and it is one of Alice's lying days, i.e. Wednesday or Thursday.

Bob says Alice's false statement is true, so Bob is lying too. Bob lies on Thursday, Friday, Sunday.

The only day in both lists is Thursday.

**Answer: (E) Thursday**

solutions.title: Test the options
solutions.body:
- Friday: Alice tells the truth, so she wouldn't say "Monday". ✗
- Sunday: Alice tells the truth. ✗
- Monday: Alice lies, so she wouldn't truthfully say "Monday". ✗
- Wednesday: Alice lies ✓, but Bob tells the truth on Wednesday and would not confirm a false statement. ✗
- Thursday: Alice lies ✓ and Bob lies ✓.

**Answer: (E) Thursday**

prompt: Werner folds a sheet of paper as shown in the figure and makes two straight cuts with a pair of scissors. He then opens up the paper again. Which of the following shapes cannot be the result?
A rectangular box solid is assembled of four pieces, as shown. Each piece consists of four cubes and is a single colour. What is the shape of the white piece?

Kanga forms two 4-digit natural numbers using each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 exactly once. Kanga wants the sum of the two numbers to be as small as possible. What is the value of this smallest possible sum?

Ms Gardner grows peas and strawberries. This year she has changed the rectangular pea bed to a square by lengthening one of its sides by 3 metres. As a result of this change, the area of the strawberry bed was reduced by 15 m². What was the area of the pea bed before the change?

Susan made a pizza in the shape of a rectangle. Then she cut it into $N$ smaller pieces by seven straight cuts. Each cut was parallel to a side of the pizza. Which of the numbers below cannot be the number, $N$, of the pieces?

solutions.title: Count rows and columns
solutions.body:
Suppose $a$ cuts are parallel to one side and $b$ to the other, $a + b = 7$. The cuts make $a+1$ strips one way and $b+1$ the other, so

$$N = (a+1)(b+1), \qquad (a+1) + (b+1) = 9.$$

Possible products: $1\cdot8 = 8$, $2\cdot7 = 14$, $3\cdot6 = 18$, $4\cdot5 = 20$.

12 cannot be obtained.

**Answer: (B) 12**

solutions.title: Check 12 directly
solutions.body:
To get 12 pieces as a grid we would need $(a+1)(b+1) = 12$ with $(a+1)+(b+1) = 9$. The factor pairs of 12 are $1\cdot12$, $2\cdot6$, $3\cdot4$ with sums 13, 8, 7 – never 9.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt: Four cards each have a number written on one side and a phrase written on the other. The four phrases are "divisible by 7", "prime", "odd" and "greater than 100", and the four numbers are 2, 5, 7 and 12. On each card, the number does not correspond to the phrase on the other side. What number is written on the same card as the phrase "greater than 100"?

In a competition to attract customers through discounts, three cell phone stores, A-cell, B-cell, and C-cell, decreased the price of a particular model that they initially sold for \$100, three times: for Christmas, Boxing Day and the New Year. A-cell decreased by 10% for Christmas, by further 20% for Boxing Day, and by another 30% in the New Year. B-cell did 20% each of the three times. Finally, C-cell reduced by 30%, then by 10%, then by 20%, respectively. At which store(s) is the phone least expensive in the New Year?

choices.text: Price is the same in all 3 stores.

solutions.title: Multiply the factors
solutions.body:
A discount of 10% multiplies the price by 0.9, 20% by 0.8, 30% by 0.7.

- A-cell: $100 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.8 \cdot 0.7 = 50.40$
- B-cell: $100 \cdot 0.8 \cdot 0.8 \cdot 0.8 = 51.20$
- C-cell: $100 \cdot 0.7 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.8 = 50.40$

A-cell and C-cell use the same three factors (order doesn't matter in multiplication), and they are cheaper than B-cell.

**Answer: (D) A-cell and C-cell**

solutions.title: Compare without the full calculation
solutions.body:
A and C apply the same discounts in a different order, so they end at the same price. Compare $0.9 \cdot 0.7 = 0.63$ with $0.8 \cdot 0.8 = 0.64$ (both also have one factor 0.8): A and C are slightly cheaper than B.

**Answer: (D) A-cell and C-cell**

prompt: Three small equilateral triangles of the same size are cut from the corners of a larger equilateral triangle with sides of 6 cm, as shown. The sum of the perimeters of the three small triangles is equal to the perimeter of the remaining grey hexagon. What is the side length of the small triangles?

A piece of cheese is cut into a large number of pieces. During the course of the day, a number of mice came and stole some pieces, watched by the lazy cat Ginger. Ginger noticed that each mouse stole a different number of pieces less than 10, and that no mouse stole exactly twice as many pieces as any other mouse. What is the largest number of mice that Ginger could have seen stealing cheese?

At the airport there is a moving walkway 500 metres long, which moves at a speed of 4 km/hour. Ann and Bill step on the walkway at the same time. Ann walks at a speed of 6 km/hour on the walkway, while Bill stands still. When Ann comes to the end of the walkway, how far is she ahead of Bill?

A magical talking square originally has sides of length 8 cm. If he tells the truth, then his sides become 2 cm shorter. If he lies, then his perimeter doubles. He makes four statements, two true and two false, in some order. What is the largest possible perimeter of the square after the four statements?

A cube is rolled on a plane so that it turns around its edges. Its bottom face passes through the positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 in that order, as shown. Which two of these positions were occupied by the same face of the cube?

Rick has five cubes. When he arranges them from smallest to largest, the difference between the heights of any two neighbouring cubes is 2 cm. The largest cube is as high as a tower built from the two smallest cubes. How high is a tower built from all five cubes?
In the diagram $ABCD$ is a square, $M$ is the midpoint of $AD$ and $MN$ is perpendicular to $AC$. What is the ratio of the area of the shaded triangle $MNC$ to the area of the square?

The tango is danced in pairs, each consisting of one man and one woman. At a dance evening no more than 50 people are present. At one moment $\frac34$ of the men are dancing with $\frac45$ of the women. How many people are dancing at that moment?

An egg timer is made of three separate hourglasses with sand, glued together to a lower and an upper wooden base. Once the timer is turned over from still, their sand runs out in 3, 4 and 5 minutes, respectively. No hourglass can be turned over separately from the others. An egg needs to boil for 7 minutes in order to be tastiest. From the still position, what is the minimum number of times one needs to turn the egg timer over, in order to measure 7 minutes accurately?

solutions.title: Find a plan with two turns
solutions.body:
**Turn 1** at time 0: all three glasses start running.

At minute 4 the 4-minute glass is empty. The 3-minute glass has been empty since minute 3 (all its sand is at the bottom).

**Turn 2** at minute 4: now the 3-minute glass has all its sand on top again and runs for exactly 3 more minutes – it empties at minute $4 + 3 = 7$.

So 7 minutes are measured from the first turn until the 3-minute glass runs out.

**One turn is not enough:** after a single turn the only moments you can observe are when a glass runs out – minutes 3, 4 and 5. None of them is 7.

**Answer: (B) 2**

solutions.title: Check every possible second turn
solutions.body:
After the first turn, the only moments we can recognise are when a glass runs out: minutes 3, 4 and 5. So the second turn must happen at one of them.

- Turn at minute 3: each glass then has exactly 3 minutes of sand on top (3-glass: all 3; 4-glass: 3 of 4 already fell; 5-glass: 3 of 5 already fell), so all run out at minute 6.
- Turn at minute 4: the 3-glass restarts and runs out at minute **7**. ✓
- Turn at minute 5: the glasses run out at minutes 8, 9 and 10.

Only turning at minute 4 works, and it uses 2 turns.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prompt: Some three-digit integers have the following property: if you remove the first digit of the number, you get a perfect square; if instead you remove the last digit of the number, you also get a perfect square. What is the sum of all the three-digit integers with this curious property?

A book contains 30 stories, each starting on a new page. The lengths of these stories are 1, 2, 3, …, 30 pages, respectively. The first story starts on the first page. What is the largest number of stories that can start on an odd-numbered page?

An equilateral triangle starts in a given position and is moved to new positions in a sequence of steps. At each step it is rotated about its centre, first by 3°, then by a further 9°, then by a further 27°, and so on (at the $n$-th step it is rotated by a further $(3^n)°$). How many different positions, including the initial position, will the triangle occupy? (Two positions are considered equal if the triangle covers the same part of the plane.)

solutions.title: Work modulo 120°
solutions.body:
An equilateral triangle rotated about its centre by $120^\circ$ covers the same region. So only the total angle modulo $120^\circ$ matters.

Total angles after each step: $0^\circ, 3^\circ, 12^\circ, 39^\circ, 120^\circ, \dots$

After 4 steps the total is $3 + 9 + 27 + 81 = 120^\circ$ – back to the start. The next rotations are $243^\circ \equiv 3^\circ$, $729^\circ \equiv 9^\circ$, $2187^\circ \equiv 27^\circ$, $6561^\circ \equiv 81^\circ \pmod{120^\circ}$ (each $3^{n+4} - 3^n = 80\cdot 3^n$ is a multiple of 120 because $3^n$ is a multiple of 3 for $n\ge1$), so the pattern repeats.

Positions: $0^\circ, 3^\circ, 12^\circ, 39^\circ$ – four different ones.

**Answer: (B) 4**

prompt: A rope is folded in half, then in half again, and then in half again. Finally the folded rope is cut through, forming several strands. The lengths of two of the strands are 4 m and 9 m. Which of the following could not have been the length of the whole rope?

A triangle is divided into four triangles and three quadrilaterals by three straight line segments, as shown. The sum of the perimeters of the three quadrilaterals is equal to 25 cm. The sum of the perimeters of the four triangles is equal to 20 cm. The perimeter of the whole triangle is equal to 19 cm. What is the sum of the lengths of the three straight line segments?

In the centre of every cell of a $5\times5$ board stands one kangaroo. Suddenly, a thunder strikes, and each kangaroo is startled so that it jumps over the side of its cell into a neighbouring cell, possibly joining one or more other kangaroos there. What is the greatest possible number of cells that are now empty?

solutions.title: Chessboard colouring
solutions.body:
Colour the board like a chessboard with the corners black: 13 black and 12 white cells. Every jump goes to a cell of the other colour. So the kangaroos from black cells land on white cells and vice versa. Number rows and columns 1–5.

**At least 5 white cells get kangaroos.** The four corner kangaroos each have only two possible target cells, and these four pairs are different: the corner (1,1) can go to (1,2) or (2,1), the corner (1,5) to (1,4) or (2,5), and so on. The kangaroo from the centre (3,3) can only go to (2,3), (3,2), (3,4), (4,3), none of which is next to a corner. So at least 5 different white cells are occupied.

**At least 4 black cells get kangaroos.** The white cells (1,2), (2,5), (5,4), (4,1) have neighbours $\{(1,1),(1,3),(2,2)\}$, $\{(1,5),(3,5),(2,4)\}$, $\{(5,5),(5,3),(4,4)\}$, $\{(5,1),(3,1),(4,2)\}$ – four disjoint sets. So their four kangaroos land on four different black cells.

Hence at least 9 cells are occupied and at most $25 - 9 = 16$ are empty.

**16 is possible:** let all black-cell kangaroos jump to the white cells (1,2), (1,4), (3,2), (4,5), (5,2) and all white-cell kangaroos jump to the black cells (1,1), (2,4), (4,2), (4,4). (Every black cell is next to one of those five white cells, and every white cell is next to one of those four black cells.) Then only 9 cells are occupied.

**Answer: (D) 16**
